questions.stem: A 39 year old man has had a cough productive of green sputum for 10 days, starting after a cold. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 84 bpm, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. His chest has scattered wheeze but no focal crackles or bronchial breathing.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A cough after a cold with wheeze but no focal signs of consolidation is acute bronchitis; green sputum does not mean pneumonia.

clues: no focal crackles or bronchial breathing
steps.x: Post-viral cough, **no focal signs**, normal observations.

elim: No focal signs, normal respiratory rate and saturation.
A chronic disease; he has a 10 day illness after a cold.
No weight loss, haemoptysis or chronic cough.
No pleuritic pain, tachycardia or hypoxia.

steps.x: **A. Acute bronchitis.** Cough after URTI + no focal signs = acute bronchitis.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman has had a cough for 8 days after a sore throat and runny nose. Her temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. She is diagnosed with acute bronchitis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on auscultation of her chest?
o: Bronchial breathing at the right base
Stony dull percussion with absent breath sounds
questions.e: Acute bronchitis gives rhonchi that clear with coughing and bilateral end-expiratory wheeze, without focal signs.

clues: cough for 8 days after a sore throat
steps.x: Bronchial inflammation with **mucus**: noises that move with a cough.

elim: A sign of consolidation (pneumonia).
Suggests pulmonary fibrosis or oedema.
Suggests pleurisy, PE or pneumonia.
Pleural effusion.

steps.x: **D. Rhonchi that clear with coughing.** Rhonchi that clear with coughing.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman has a cough with clear sputum and mild chest discomfort for 6 days. It began after a common cold that her children also had. Her chest has mild bilateral wheeze only. Her GP diagnoses acute bronchitis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Acute bronchitis is almost always viral; rhinovirus is the commonest cause.

steps.x: Post-cold bronchitis: think **virus**.

elim: Whooping cough gives paroxysms with a whoop and vomiting.
Bacterial; bronchitis is almost always viral.
Causes atypical pneumonia, usually with systemic features.
The commonest cause of pneumonia, not bronchitis.

steps.x: **D. Rhinovirus.** Rhinovirus is the most common cause.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man was diagnosed with acute bronchitis 1 week ago. He now has a temperature of 39.4°C, new breathlessness and right-sided chest pain on breathing in. His pulse rate is 108 bpm, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. There is dullness and bronchial breathing at the right base.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication?
questions.e: High fever, breathlessness, chest pain and focal signs after bronchitis mean progression to pneumonia, its main complication.

clues: diagnosed with acute bronchitis 1 week ago
bronchial breathing at the right base
steps.x: Bronchitis has now developed **emergency features** and **focal consolidation**.

elim: No asthma history and focal signs point elsewhere.
Usually follows aspiration with weeks of swinging fever and foul sputum.
Would give hyper-resonance, not dullness and bronchial breathing.
Bronchitis has no focal signs and only mild fever.

steps.x: **D. Secondary bacterial pneumonia.** High fever + breathless + chest pain = progression to pneumonia.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has had a cough and mild fever for 9 days. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 86 bpm, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. She has scattered wheeze. A chest X-ray (see item resources) has been taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Bronchitis inflames the airways without alveolar consolidation, so the CXR is clear.

clues: cough and mild fever for 9 days
steps.x: Cough, mild fever, wheeze and a **clear CXR**.

elim: Causes chronic daily purulent sputum over years.
The CXR shows no consolidation.
No weight loss, night sweats or upper zone changes.
Would show bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.

steps.x: **A. Acute bronchitis.** Bronchitis: airway inflammation, no consolidation.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man has acute bronchitis, with a cough productive of clear sputum for 7 days. His chest has mild wheeze only. His GP reviews his history.
questions.q: Which feature is the most likely risk factor for his illness?
o: Upper respiratory tract infection 1 week ago
questions.e: Recent URTI and smoking are the risk factors for acute bronchitis.

steps.x: What precedes viral bronchitis?

elim: Associated with asthma, not bronchitis.
Risk factor for VTE.
Associated with endocarditis or aspiration, not bronchitis.
Irrelevant.

steps.x: **D. Upper respiratory tract infection 1 week ago.** Recent URTI and smoking.

questions.stem: A 44 year old teacher has had a dry cough for 3 weeks. It started with a cold and sore throat. She now feels well apart from the cough, which is worse at night. Her temperature is 36.9°C and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. Her chest is clear. She has no weight loss.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Post-viral bronchitis cough can last several weeks; a clear chest with normal observations fits.

steps.x: Cough lasting **weeks** after a viral URTI, now otherwise well.

elim: No previous wheeze or atopy; cough started with a cold.
No heartburn; cough began with a viral illness.
No weight loss, and a 3 week cough that began with a cold is post-viral.
No paroxysms, whoop or post-tussive vomiting.

steps.x: **A. Acute bronchitis.** Bronchitis cough can last weeks.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with acute bronchitis returns to his GP on day 8. He now has a temperature of 38.9°C, breathlessness on walking and new left-sided chest pain. His respiratory rate is 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. His chest X-ray (see item resources) is shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Emergency features (high fever, breathlessness, chest pain) plus CXR consolidation mean bronchitis has progressed to pneumonia.

steps.x: Bronchitis with **red-flag** features and an abnormal CXR.

elim: No oedema on CXR and fever points to infection.
A short febrile illness with consolidation.
The CXR shows consolidation, not a meniscus.
CXR shows consolidation and the history is infective.

steps.x: **D. Pneumonia complicating acute bronchitis.** Red flags + consolidation = pneumonia.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man had acute bronchitis 4 weeks ago. The fever has gone and he feels well, but a dry cough persists, triggered by cold air. His temperature is 36.8°C and his chest is clear.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his persistent cough?
questions.e: Post-bronchitic cough persists for weeks because of airway epithelial inflammation and hyperresponsiveness after the virus clears.

steps.x: Well, afebrile, clear chest: a **post-viral** cough.

elim: He is afebrile, well and has a clear chest.
COPD is a chronic smoking disease, not a post-viral cough.
The virus has cleared; inflammation persists.
Fibrosis gives progressive breathlessness and crackles.

steps.x: **C. Ongoing airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness.** Lingering cough = airway hyperresponsiveness.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has had a cough productive of yellow sputum for 5 days after a cold. Her temperature is 37.7°C, pulse rate 90 bpm, respiratory rate 17 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. Auscultation reveals bilateral end-expiratory wheeze with no crackles. Percussion is resonant throughout.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Bilateral end-expiratory wheeze with no focal signs after a cold is acute bronchitis.

clues: bilateral end-expiratory wheeze with no crackles
steps.x: Airway signs only, **no consolidation**.

elim: No COPD history.
An infant illness caused by RSV.
Resonant percussion and no crackles exclude consolidation.
Percussion is resonant.

steps.x: **A. Acute bronchitis.** Bilateral wheeze, no focal signs = bronchitis.

questions.stem: A 23 year old student has had a cough with clear sputum for 6 days after a cold. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 78 bpm, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. Her chest has mild wheeze that clears with coughing.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Acute bronchitis is a clinical diagnosis made on history and examination alone.

steps.x: Typical bronchitis in a **well** young patient.

elim: Only if pneumonia is suspected or the diagnosis is uncertain.
Not needed in a well, low-risk patient.
Not used in acute infection.
Bronchitis is viral; not needed.

steps.x: **C. No investigation required.** Clinical diagnosis: no tests needed.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has had a cough for 10 days after a cold. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. There are crackles at the left base. The GP is unsure whether he has bronchitis or pneumonia.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: A chest X-ray is used to exclude pneumonia when the diagnosis is uncertain.

clues: unsure whether he has bronchitis or pneumonia
steps.x: Diagnosis **uncertain**: is there consolidation?

elim: Invasive; not used to separate bronchitis from pneumonia.
For suspected PE.
Not used acutely.
For TB, not suggested here.

steps.x: **B. Chest X-ray.** CXR excludes pneumonia when unsure.

questions.stem: A 41 year old man has acute bronchitis after a cold. He is well, with a temperature of 37.3°C and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. He asks for a sputum test 'to find out which antibiotic will work'.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain it is a clinical diagnosis and usually viral
Send throat swab for bacterial culture
questions.e: Bronchitis is diagnosed clinically; it is almost always viral so tests and antibiotics are not needed.

steps.x: Typical, **low-risk** bronchitis.

elim: Not needed when the diagnosis is clear.
Bronchitis is viral; culture does not help.
Not indicated.
Antibiotics are not indicated.

steps.x: **B. Explain it is a clinical diagnosis and usually viral.** No tests: clinical, viral diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman has had a productive cough for 2 weeks after a cold. She now has a temperature of 38.6°C and feels more breathless. Her respiratory rate is 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. There are coarse crackles at the right base.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Worsening fever, breathlessness and focal crackles suggest pneumonia; a CXR excludes it.

clues: coarse crackles at the right base
steps.x: Bronchitis possibly **progressing to pneumonia**.

elim: Not indicated in an infective picture.
Not first-line.
For asthma.
Red-flag features need assessment now.

steps.x: **A. Chest X-ray.** Uncertain diagnosis = CXR.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has had a cough productive of green sputum for 7 days after a cold, with a mild fever. She has no medical history. Her temperature is 37.7°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. Her chest has scattered rhonchi.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Most bronchitis needs reassurance, self-care and paracetamol or ibuprofen; green sputum alone is not an indication for antibiotics.

steps.x: Low-risk, well patient.

elim: Antibiotics are not needed in low-risk patients.
Reserved for high-risk patients.
No role in bronchitis.
No asthma; inhaled steroid not indicated.

steps.x: **D. Paracetamol, fluids and reassurance.** Self-care and analgesia.

questions.stem: An 83 year old woman has had a productive cough for 9 days after a cold. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 88 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. Her chest has scattered rhonchi but no focal signs. She has no allergies.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Age over 80 makes her high risk, so antibiotics are offered: doxycycline for 5 days first-line.

steps.x: Bronchitis in someone **over 80**.

elim: For severe hospital pneumonia, not bronchitis.
Not first-line and too long.
No role.
Age over 80 is a high-risk feature.

steps.x: **C. Oral doxycycline for 5 days.** High risk = doxycycline 5 days.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man has had a cough for 8 days after a cold. He is otherwise well with no medical history. His temperature is 37.9°C and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. The chest has no focal signs. A point-of-care CRP is shown.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: CRP over 100 mg/L puts him in the antibiotic group; doxycycline for 5 days is first-line.

clues: otherwise well with no medical history
steps.x: No comorbidity or age criterion, but **CRP above 100**.

elim: Not indicated.
CRP above 100 mg/L is an indication for antibiotics.
Not the antibiotic of choice for bronchitis.
A urinary antibiotic.

steps.x: **C. Oral doxycycline for 5 days.** CRP >100 = offer antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 25 year old woman with asthma has acute bronchitis after a cold. She has a cough and wheeze that is waking her at night. Her temperature is 37.5°C and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Peak flow is 85% of her best.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate addition to her treatment?
questions.e: A short-acting bronchodilator helps wheeze in bronchitis, particularly with underlying airway disease such as asthma.

steps.x: Bronchitis with wheeze on a background of **asthma**.

elim: Not needed in a low-risk patient.
Not first-line; may suppress respiration.
Not used for acute bronchitis.
For an asthma exacerbation with reduced peak flow; hers is 85%.

steps.x: **A. Inhaled salbutamol as needed.** Salbutamol for wheeze in underlying airway disease.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man has acute bronchitis. He has a dry cough keeping him awake for 6 nights, with no wheeze. His temperature is 37.2°C and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. He takes paracetamol already and asks for something to help the cough.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate option?
questions.e: Simple cough suppressants such as dextromethorphan can be used if needed, alongside analgesia.

steps.x: Symptom relief for **cough** with no wheeze.

elim: Antibiotics do not help viral bronchitis.
No airway disease.
No role.
Bronchodilators only help if there is wheeze or airway disease.

steps.x: **A. Dextromethorphan.** Simple cough suppressant if needed.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man with heart failure has a cough productive of sputum for 6 days after a cold. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 90 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. His chest has scattered wheeze and no focal signs.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Refer for chest X-ray before deciding
questions.e: Comorbidities such as heart failure or type 2 diabetes make him high risk, so antibiotics (doxycycline 5 days) are offered.

steps.x: Bronchitis with a **high-risk comorbidity**.

elim: He has an infection, not decompensated heart failure.
Not first-line for bronchitis.
Heart failure is a high-risk comorbidity.
No focal signs; the diagnosis is clear.

steps.x: **B. Oral doxycycline for 5 days.** Comorbidity = antibiotics (doxycycline).

questions.stem: A 33 year old man has acute bronchitis after a cold. A student asks why his chest X-ray is normal when he has a productive cough.
questions.q: Which best explains the normal chest X-ray?
o: Bacteria have not yet reached the lungs
Inflammation is confined to the bronchial epithelium
Pleural inflammation is not seen on X-ray
The alveoli are filled with exudate
The X-ray was taken too early
questions.e: Viral infection of the tracheobronchial epithelium causes inflammation and mucus without alveolar consolidation, which distinguishes it from pneumonia.

clues: normal when he has a productive cough
steps.x: Productive cough, **clear CXR**.

elim: Bronchitis is viral.
Bronchitis does not involve the pleura.
That is consolidation, seen in pneumonia.
Bronchitis does not progress to consolidation unless complicated.

steps.x: **B. Inflammation is confined to the bronchial epithelium.** Airways inflamed, alveoli clear.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman with acute bronchitis asks for antibiotics. She is well, with a temperature of 37.4°C and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air, and has no medical history. Her GP declines to prescribe.
questions.q: Which best explains why antibiotics are not indicated?
o: Bacteria in bronchitis are always resistant
She has had symptoms for too long
The cause is almost always viral
questions.e: Bronchitis is viral, so antibiotics give little benefit; they are reserved for high-risk groups where bacterial superinfection is likely or dangerous.

steps.x: Low-risk patient: why not antibiotics?

elim: They do.
Untrue; the cause is viral.
Duration is not the reason.
Bronchitis is viral.

steps.x: **D. The cause is almost always viral.** Viral cause = antibiotics little benefit.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man had acute bronchitis 5 weeks ago. His cough has improved but still occurs on exercise and in cold air. Spirometry is normal. A student asks why.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
questions.e: After viral bronchitis the airway epithelium stays inflamed and hyperresponsive even once the virus has cleared.

steps.x: Prolonged cough triggered by irritants after the infection.

elim: He is well; no infection.
Spirometry is normal.
Not caused by bronchitis.
The virus has cleared.

steps.x: **B. Bronchial hyperresponsiveness after viral injury.** Post-viral hyperresponsiveness.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has acute bronchitis and is prescribed doxycycline. Her neighbour, aged 40 and well, had the same illness and was not given antibiotics. She asks why.
questions.q: Which best explains the difference?
o: Bacterial superinfection is more likely or more dangerous in her
questions.e: Antibiotics are reserved for high-risk groups where bacterial superinfection is more likely or more dangerous.

steps.x: Same viral illness, different **risk**.

elim: Untrue.
Doxycycline is antibacterial.
She has bronchitis.
Both are almost certainly viral.

steps.x: **A. Bacterial superinfection is more likely or more dangerous in her.** High risk = antibiotics for possible superinfection.
